Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:31: We learn in Avot D'Rabbi Natan (cf. 15:1): and Rabbi Eliezer used to say two further things: let your fellow's honor be as precious to you as your own; be careful of the honor of his sons and daughters. If you want no one to take what is yours, do not take what is your fellow's. If you want no one to speak of you, do not speak of your fellow.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:32: Hillel says, be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving the creatures and drawing them near to Torah. A person is obligated to love his fellow and give him honor — and is this not a kal vachomer: if the ministering angels, among whom there is no evil inclination, give one another honor, then flesh and blood, among whom the evil inclination is present, how much more so — as it is said (Isaiah 6:3), "and one called to the other and said" — one says to his fellow, "you are greater than I, and you open the praise of the Omnipresent first."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:33: We learn in Megillat Chasidim (cf. Masechet DeRabbi Eliezer Zuta ch. 2): do you wish to acquire a friend for yourself? Deal generously in his welfare. And a person should not act against his fellow's wishes, and should set aside his own will for the will of others, as we learn in tractate Shabbat (118b): Rabbi Yosi said, in all my days I never acted against the wishes of my colleagues; I know I am not a Kohen, but had my colleagues told me to go up to the platform [to give the priestly blessing], I would have gone up.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:34: There are eight categories of people; whoever associates with one learns a distinct quality of its own. These are they: 1) whoever associates with kings learns violence and pride; 2) whoever associates with the wealthy learns love of money and the pleasure of this world; 3) whoever associates with the humble learns humility, praise, and thanksgiving; 4) whoever associates with women learns lewdness, desire, laughter, obscene speech, and every evil thought; 5) whoever associates with youths learns idle talk and frivolity, as we learn (Avot 3:10), the idle talk of children and sitting in the assemblies of the unlearned drive a person from the world; 6) whoever associates with the wicked learns sins and transgressions and has repentance removed from him; 7) whoever associates with scoffers learns falsehood and lies; 8) whoever associates with the pious and the righteous learns kindness and good qualities and inherits the World to Come. A person should always strive to acquire a friend for himself — if he can find one for free, [well and good]; if not, he should acquire one with money, as we learn (Avot 1:6), make yourself a teacher and acquire for yourself a friend. And the sage said, I am amazed that a person acquires slaves with his money — how does he not acquire free men with his good words, since with good words a person acquires friends more than with money?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:35: The early pious ones used to judge every person favorably, and even if they saw a person doing something that appeared to many as a transgression, they would not disgrace him in their hearts, but would judge him favorably, saying, perhaps he did not transgress and his intent was for something else, and they would remove themselves from suspicion, for whoever suspects the innocent is afflicted in his body (Shabbat 97a). We learn in tractate Shabbat (127b): our Rabbis taught, whoever judges his fellow favorably is himself judged favorably — a story of a certain man from the Upper Galilee, etc.; see there. And another story of Rabbi Yehoshua, etc.; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:36: We learn in Avot D'Rabbi Natan: judge every person favorably — a story of a man who sent his son to his fellow and said, "my father says, lend me a measure of wheat." He went and found him measuring wheat, and he said, "I have none." He came and told his father, who said, "perhaps it was tithe-produce." Again he told him, "go tell him, my father says, lend me one maneh." He went and found him counting money, and he said, "I have none." He came and told his father, who said, "perhaps it was a deposit in his keeping." When they later met in the marketplace, his fellow said to him, "when your son came and found me measuring wheat and I did not give it to you, what did you suspect me of?" He said, "perhaps it was tithe-produce." "And when he found me counting money, what did you suspect me of?" He said, "perhaps it was a deposit." He said to him, "I swear, so it was, and you did not veer right or left, and of you it is said, judge every person favorably; and just as you judged me favorably, so may the Holy One, blessed be He, judge you favorably."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:37: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, whoever suspects the innocent is afflicted in his own body (Shabbat 97a). From where do we learn this? From Moses, who said (Exodus 4:1), "but they will not believe me" — and it was known before Heaven that they would believe, as it is said (ibid. 4:31), "and the people believed." And since he suspected them, Moses was immediately punished, as it is written (ibid. 4:6), "and the LORD said to him further" [giving him a sign] — was there not another matter [needed] besides tzara'at in his own body? Rather, from here we learn that he was punished for this matter. Rava said, and some say Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina: the measure of good comes more swiftly than the measure of punishment — for there [regarding the punishment] (ibid.), "and he brought it out, and behold, his hand was leprous like snow" — in the measure of punishment it lingered and it says "and behold, his hand was leprous" [a fuller description], but in the measure of good it did not linger and does not say "and behold, his hand," but simply "and behold, it had returned like his flesh" (ibid. 4:7).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:38: And one who is suspected of something he did not do should extricate himself from suspicion (cf. Berachot 31b) — for so we find with Chana, to whom Eli said (1 Samuel 1:14-15), "how long will you be drunk?" and she said to him, "no, my lord, I am a woman of sorrowful spirit; I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink" — immediately he said to her, "go in peace." From here we learn that one who suspects a person of something he did not do must appease him — and moreover, he must seek mercy for him, as it is said (ibid. 1:17), "and may the God of Israel grant your request" (Berachot there). Rabbi Yosi said, may my portion be with one who is suspected of something he did not do (Shabbat 118b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:39: Whoever loves his fellow always judges him favorably and covers over his transgressions; but if he hates him, he always judges him unfavorably even if he has not sinned, and finds no merit in him even though he is upright, and through this quarrels with him and seeks grievance against him — as it is said (Proverbs 10:12), "hatred stirs up strife, but love covers over all transgressions." For because he hates him, his words appear suspect to him, and he quarrels with him for no reason; the opposite is true if he loves him — even if his fellow is bound to him by covenant and oath, he will renege and break the covenant, since the hatred hidden in his heart will search out quarrels and stir up strife and every hatred and rivalry; and he thinks in his heart that his fellow also hates him, for he judges the hearts of others as being evil like his own evil heart, and he thinks that the evil fantasies in his own heart are likewise in others' hearts, and from evil thought he comes to action and hates the creatures. This is like a man walking on a narrow path — if that place is not high above the ground, he will walk swiftly and not stumble, all the more so not fall; but if that place is high above the ground, he will think in his heart that he will fall to the ground, and out of his fear of falling, it comes to pass. Likewise with one who fantasizes something evil in his heart — it will appear to him that what he fantasized is true and it will become established in his heart and come to pass; and likewise most dreams are nothing but the fantasies a person entertains in his heart while awake, which are shown to him in a dream.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:40: We learn in the Midrash: "behold, Pharaoh's army that came out to help you shall return to its own land, to Egypt" (Jeremiah 37:7) — why did Pharaoh's army return to Egypt and not come to help Israel? Because they hated them — when they reached the edge of the sea and fantasized in their hearts their hatred of Israel, from the evil thought and hatred and fantasy, there appeared to them at the sea's edge inflated waterskins floating on the surface of the water, and they immediately turned back, thinking these were the bodies of their fathers whom the Holy One, blessed be He, had drowned in the sea through Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, and they said, it is a disgrace for us to help our enemies who drowned our fathers in the sea after inflicting several plagues upon them. From this we learn that hatred brings about enmity and strife.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:41: We learn in the Sifrei: "when men strive" (Deuteronomy 25:11) — no peace comes out of strife, as it says (Genesis 13:7), "and there was strife between the herdsmen of Abram's cattle and the herdsmen of Lot's cattle." What caused Lot to separate from Abraham the righteous? Say, strife. Likewise it says (Deuteronomy 19:17), "and the two men who have the dispute shall stand" — what caused him to be struck [with punishment]? Say, strife. This teaches only of two men — from where do we include a mother and daughter, or a man and woman? The verse teaches "together."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:42: Therefore a person must restrain himself from strife, for whoever restrains himself from strife is honored among people, as it is said (Proverbs 20:3), "it is an honor for a man to cease from strife." And it is written (ibid. 12:26), "the righteous man has more than his fellow, but the way of the wicked leads them astray" — meaning, the righteous man has an advantage over another person, since the righteous man hears his own disgrace and endures it, subduing his craving and his inclination and remaining silent so as not to come to strife and disgrace; "but the way of the wicked leads them astray" — the evil way of the wicked leads them astray, for it seems a disgrace to them to hear their own reproach and remain silent, and they stray from the path of reason, so that through this they come to quarreling and murder. And we learn in Chullin (cf. 89a): Rabbi Ila'i said, the world is sustained only through the merit of one who restrains his mouth at a time of strife, as we copied his words above in chapter 3. And the sage said, no one has ever disgraced me more than once, for the first time I bear his disgrace, and he does not disgrace me a second time.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:43: We learn in the Midrash: "a man of friends must show himself friendly" (Proverbs 18:24) — whoever wants to have friends must bear and overlook his own way and receive them with a pleasant countenance. Meaning, "lehitro'ea" [to show friendliness] derives from "rea" [companion] — meaning, he should make himself a companion and friend to all people. Another interpretation of "ish re'im" etc.: a person will never have friends unless he humbles himself before them and breaks his craving — from the root of (Psalms 2:9), "you shall break them [ter'em] with a rod of iron" — and thus his companionship will be fitting and complete. And the sage said, whoever does not break his pride before his fellow, and is not always insulted by them without ever insulting any of them, will not have friends.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:44: These good qualities cause a person to have friends more beloved than his own brothers, as it is said (Proverbs 18:24), "but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother," and it is written (ibid. 27:10), "do not forsake your friend or your father's friend." If you keep this and do not forsake your friend or your father's friend, you will not need your brother in your day of calamity, for your companion will save you in your day of distress, being to you more than a brother.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:45: We learn in Shemot Rabbah (27:1): "better a close neighbor" — this is Yitro; "than a distant brother" — this is Esau. Of Yitro it is written (1 Samuel 15:6), "and you did kindness with all the children of Israel" etc.; of Esau it is written (Deuteronomy 25:17), "remember what Amalek did to you." You find many things proving that they are written of Esau in disgrace and of Yitro in praise: of Esau it is written (Lamentations 5:11), "they raped women in Zion"; of Yitro it is written (Exodus 2:21), "and he gave Zipporah his daughter to Moses." Of Esau it is written (Psalms 14:4), "who devour my people, they have eaten bread"; of Yitro it is written (Exodus 2:20), "call him, that he may eat bread." Of Esau it is written (Deuteronomy 25:18), "and he did not fear God"; of Yitro it is written (Exodus 18:23), "and God will command you." Esau nullified sacrifices; of Yitro it is written (ibid. 18:12), "and Yitro took a burnt offering and sacrifices" etc. Esau heard of their going out and came to fight against them, as it is said (ibid. 17:8), "and Amalek came"; while Yitro heard of their well-being and came and attached himself to them, as it is said (ibid. 18:1), "and Yitro heard" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:46: Righteous converts are equal to Israel in love and are like Israel in all their matters, and it is a positive commandment to love the convert, as it is said (Deuteronomy 10:19), "and you shall love the convert." We learn in the Mechilta (on Exodus 22:20): "and you shall not wrong a convert" — do not wrong him with words, and do not oppress him with money. With words — that you should not say to him, "just yesterday you worshipped idols with pig fat still gleaming between your teeth, and now you stand and speak against me!" And if you wrong him, he will wrong you, as it is said, "for you were converts in the land of Egypt." From here Rabbi Natan used to say, do not point out to your fellow the very blemish that is in you [yourself].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:47: We learn in Bava Metzia (59b): our Rabbis taught, whoever wrongs a convert transgresses three negative commandments, and whoever oppresses him transgresses two. It was taught, Rabbi Eliezer says, why did the Torah warn regarding the convert in thirty-six places? Because it is written [there] "for you were converts."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:48: Beloved are converts, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, weighs equal to the holiness of Shabbat and the holiness [i.e., prohibition] against idolatry — for the verse warns regarding Shabbat in twenty-eight places, and regarding idolatry in twenty-eight places, and regarding the convert too it warns in twenty-eight places.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:49: Israel are called holy, as it is said (Deuteronomy 14:2), "for you are a holy people," through their sanctifying themselves from idolatry, as it is said (Leviticus 20:7), "and you shall sanctify yourselves and you shall be holy" — from idolatry, from carrion and torn animals, and from detestable and creeping things, from impurities. From idolatry, as it is said at the end of the portion of forbidden relations, "and you shall sanctify yourselves"; from carrion and torn animals, as it is said (Exodus 22:30), "and you shall be holy men to Me"; from detestable and creeping things, as it is said at the end of the portion of forbidden foods (Leviticus 11:44), "for I am the LORD your God, and you shall sanctify yourselves and you shall be holy"; from impurities, as it is said (ibid. 16:19), "and shall cleanse it and sanctify it from the impurities of the children of Israel." Even in the future to come, the Holy One, blessed be He, will sanctify them, as it is said (Ezekiel 37:28), "and the nations shall know that I, the LORD, sanctify Israel" — and likewise it says "and you shall be holy to Me" in this world, "and I have separated you from the peoples to be Mine" in the World to Come. Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus says, had it said "and I will separate the peoples from you," there would have been no future existence for the nations of the world and no opening for any of them to convert — to what is this comparable? To one who sorts bad from good; he does not return to the bad ones lest he find some good among them [likewise, the possibility of conversion remains open].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:50: Beloved are converts, for in many places [the Torah] equates them with Israel. Israel are called servants, as it is said (Leviticus 25:55), "for the children of Israel are servants to Me"; and converts are called servants, as it is said (Isaiah 56:6), "and the sons of the stranger who join themselves to the LORD, to serve Him and to love the name of the LORD, to be His servants." Israel are called ministers, as it is said (ibid. 61:6), "but you shall be called priests of the LORD, ministers of our God shall you be called"; and converts are called ministers, as it is said, "and the sons of the stranger who join themselves to the LORD to serve/minister to Him." Israel are called beloved, as it is said (Malachi 1:2), "I have loved you, says the LORD"; and converts are called beloved, as it is said (Deuteronomy 10:18), "and He loves the convert." Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says, "and those who love Him are like the sun going forth" (Judges 5:31) — whoever loves the Omnipresent, the Omnipresent loves him; of converts it is written "and He loves the convert," and of the righteous it is written "and those who love Him are like the sun going forth in its might." Now, who is greater — one who loves the king, or one whom the king loves? By way of parable: all love their king, but fortunate is he whom his king loves.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:51: Onkelos the convert asked Rabbi Eliezer, saying, is all the affection the Holy One, blessed be He, shows the convert only to give him "bread and a garment" (Deuteronomy 10:18)? He said to him, is this a small thing in your eyes? A thing over which that elder [Jacob] pleaded, saying (Genesis 28:20), "and give me bread to eat" etc. He came before Rabbi Yehoshua, who began to appease him, saying to him, "bread" here means the bread of Torah, as it is said (Proverbs 9:5), "come, eat of my bread"; and "garment" is Torah, as it is said (Isaiah 3:6), "you shall have this garment, be our leader." Moreover, their daughters marry into the priesthood and bear priests, and thereby merit "bread and garment" [in a fuller sense] — "bread" being the showbread, and "garment" the priestly vestments — this is in the Temple; and from where do we learn this also applies outside [the Land]? "Bread" is challah [the tithe of dough], and "garment" is the first shearing [given to the priest].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:52: Of Israel it is said "covenant," as it is said (Genesis 17:13), "and My covenant shall be in your flesh"; and of converts it is said "covenant," as it is said (Isaiah 56:4), "and hold fast to My covenant." Of Israel it is said "favor," as it is said (Exodus 28:38), "for favor for them before the LORD"; and of converts it is said "favor," as it is said (Isaiah 56:7), "their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be for favor on My altar." Of Israel it is said "guarding," as it is said (Psalms 121:3), "behold, He who guards Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps"; and of converts it is said "guarding," as it is said (ibid. 146:9), "the LORD guards the converts." And you likewise find converts among the four groups that answer before Him who spoke and the world came into being (Isaiah 44:5): "one shall say, I am the LORD's" — these are Israel; "and this one shall call by the name of Jacob" — these are righteous converts; "and this one shall write with his hand, to the LORD" — these are penitents; "and shall be surnamed by the name of Israel" — these are those who fear Heaven.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:53: Rabbi says, a convert who comes to convert is as though he has done a kindness with all of Israel — for so Saul says to the sons of Yitro (1 Samuel 15:6), "and you did kindness with all the children of Israel" — is there anyone who can do kindness with all those thousands and myriads? Rather, since he converted among them, [it is] as it is said (Exodus 18:10), "blessed be the LORD who saved you" — as though he had done a kindness with all of them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:54: Beloved are converts, for the Holy One, blessed be He, adds to their name — for you find that Yitro was at first called only "Yeter," as it is said (Exodus 4:18), "and he returned to Yeter, his father-in-law"; but once he converted, he was called "Yitro" [with an added letter]. And so too, whoever rises to greatness has something added to his name, as it is said (Genesis 17:5), "and your name shall be Abraham," and likewise (Numbers 13:16), "and Moses called Hoshea son of Nun, Joshua." And some have their names diminished because of their evil deeds — for Achav, the false prophet, is called "Achab" [shortened], as it is said (Jeremiah 29:21-22), "may God make you like Tzidkiyahu and like Achab."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:55: A convert who converts is given reward as one who has toiled in Torah all his days, as it is said (Numbers 10:29), "come with us, and we will do you good" — [treating him] as one of us. And when he came to Joshua and set aside the produce of Jericho and all its yield for the Temple, he said, whoever's inheritance the building of the Temple falls within shall take this in place of [what would otherwise support] the Temple; and who ate it all those years? The sons of Yitro, as it is said (Judges 1:16), "and the children of the Kenite, Moses's father-in-law, went up from the city of palms" — teaching that they dwelt there as long as Joshua lived, since they were available to teach Torah, and they arose and turned from there, as it is said, "they went up from the city of palms," and they went about seeking someone to teach them Torah, and found Yabetz and settled near him, as it is said (1 Chronicles 2:55), "and the families of the scribes who dwelt at Yabetz: the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, the Sucathites — these are the Kenites" etc. "Tirathites" — because they would sound an alarm [matri'in] in their petitions and be answered. "Shimeathites" — because their prayer was heard [nishma'at]. "Sucathites" — because they would shelter and protect [mesakhkhin] all of Israel. Come and see the righteousness of the sons of Yitro — for Yonadav ben Rechav heard from the mouth of the prophet in the Temple that it was destined to be destroyed, and he decreed upon his children three decrees: 1) that they not drink wine, 2) that they not build houses, 3) that they not plant vineyards — as it is said (Jeremiah 35:6), "and they said, we will not drink wine, for Yonadav ben Rechav our father commanded us." Rabbi Yochanan says, greater is the covenant made with the sons of Yitro than the covenant made with David — for that covenant [with David] was conditional: "if your children keep My covenant, and if not, I will visit their transgression with the rod" (Psalms 89:33); but the covenant made with Yonadav was not conditional, as it is said (Jeremiah 35:19), "a man of the line of Yonadav ben Rechav shall not be cut off" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:56: And further we learn in Shemot Rabbah: "and Yitro heard" — this is what is written (Jeremiah 16:19), "O LORD, my strength, my stronghold, and my refuge." Israel said before the Holy One, blessed be He: at the time You performed miracles for us at the sea, we said, "my strength and song is Yah" (Exodus 15:2); Rachab heard and came to attach herself to You, as it is said (Joshua 2:10), "for we have heard how [the LORD] dried up" — hence, "O LORD, my strength and my stronghold." When You performed miracles in the days of Solomon, as it is written (1 Samuel 2:10), "and He will give strength to His king," the Queen of Sheba came and praised You — what did she say? (1 Kings 10:9), "blessed be the LORD your God." When You brought us out of Egypt and gave us the Torah, called "strength," as it is said (Psalms 29:11), "the LORD will give strength to His people," Yitro heard and came and attached himself to You — hence (Jeremiah 16:19), "to You the nations shall come from the ends of the earth."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:57: We learn in Bamidbar Rabbah: to what are converts comparable in relation to Israel? To a shepherd who was tending his flock, and a ewe escaped from the field and came and joined his flock, and it was more precious to him than the others — because his flock he had purchased with money, while this one he had not purchased, but she came of her own accord and joined his flock. So it is with Israel: how many signs, wonders, and marvels did the Holy One, blessed be He, perform for them, and only then did they accept the Torah; but this convert comes of his own accord to enter under the wings of the Shechinah without a sign or wonder.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:58: Beloved are converts, for all the Patriarchs called themselves converts. Abraham, peace be upon him, said (Genesis 23:4), "a stranger [ger] and sojourner am I among you." Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said (Exodus 2:22), "I have been a stranger [ger] in a foreign land." King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 39:13), "for I am a stranger [ger] with You." And Isaac our father, peace be upon him, too is called a "stranger," as it is said (Genesis 26:6), "and Isaac dwelt in Gerar [related to ger]." And Jacob our father, peace be upon him, too is called a stranger (ibid. 47:4), "we have come to sojourn [lagur] in the land." Our fathers called themselves strangers, as it is written (1 Chronicles 29:15), "for we are strangers before You."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:59: Beloved are converts, for their sake the Holy One, blessed be He, delayed with Abraham regarding circumcision until he reached ninety-nine years — for had Abraham been circumcised at ten or twenty years of age, there would have been a fixed limit to the matter, and a convert could only convert up to that age; instead the Holy One, blessed be He, delayed ninety-nine years until he completed a hundred, in order to give an opening for all who come into the world to convert [at any age]. Therefore a person must love converts and have compassion on them, saying, this one who left his father, mother, family, and native land, and came to enter under the wings of the Shechinah, deserves compassion. And whoever does not have compassion on him is shown no compassion from Heaven.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:60: Whoever is cruel and lacks compassion, hates the creatures, and strikes his fellow with the whip of his tongue and the words of his mouth, his sin and punishment are exceedingly great — all the more so one who raises his hand against his fellow, and all the more so with a sword or spear, as we learn in Sanhedrin (cf. 58b): Rabbi Chanina said, whoever slaps his fellow's cheek is as though he slaps the cheek of the Shechinah, as it is said (Proverbs 20:25), "it is a snare for a man to hastily [ye'la] declare a thing holy" [read as a play on "laoa," cheek].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:61: We learn in Midrash Mishlei (22:11): "he who loves a pure heart, whose speech is gracious" etc. — meaning, whoever loves his companions in his heart and speaks softly to them with his lips deserves to be a friend to a king. And Rabbi Chananel, of blessed memory, explained "his friend is the king," meaning his words are heeded more than the words of the king — for the king's words are heeded out of fear, but the pure-hearted person's words are heeded because of his gracious speech. And by the response of one's mouth, the one who loves is recognized, just as the hater is recognized by his lips, as it is said (Proverbs 26:24), "a hater is recognized by his lips." Another interpretation of "a hater is recognized by his lips": meaning, he does not show the hatred in his heart, but graces his words, while within him lies deceit; and "recognized" means he shows in his mouth the opposite of what is in his heart, as in "and he made himself unrecognizable to them" (Genesis 42:7), and "even by his deeds a child makes himself recognizable" (Proverbs 20:11).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:62: A person must honor his fellow even if he is lesser than him in wisdom and years, and our Sages of blessed memory went to great lengths regarding this, saying (Avot 2:10), Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua says, let the honor of your student be as precious to you as your own, and the honor of your fellow like the reverence for your teacher, and the reverence for your teacher like the reverence for Heaven.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:63: A person is obligated to instruct his fellow and guide him on the good path, and love him as his own soul; and if he asked something of his fellow and he did not fulfill his wish, he should not blame him. The sage said, if I asked something of my friend and he did not fulfill my request, I would say my request was not fulfilled because of my own unworthiness, and I forgive my friend for not fulfilling it. He should not intend the benefit of his fellow except for the sake of Heaven, not so that people praise him. And if his fellow sins against him or does something improper to him, even if it causes him great distress, he should remove the anger from his heart and forgive him immediately. But if he himself has sinned against his fellow, he should multiply overtures to him until he appeases him — and even his enemy who caused him great distress, he should repay good for evil. Know that a person's misfortune in this world comes only from his own sins, and a person has no ability to cause distress to his fellow unless he has assistance from above through the other's sin; therefore he should not blame his fellow but rather his own sin and transgression, as it is said (Isaiah 50:1), "behold, for your iniquities you were sold."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:64: A person should always draw near those who love him and distance himself from those who hate him, and should listen to and accept the counsel of those who love him, as we learn in Yevamot (62b): whoever loves his neighbors, draws his relatives near, marries his sister's daughter, and lends to a poor person in his time of need — of him the verse says (Isaiah 58:9), "then you shall call, and the LORD will answer." And even though his relatives curse and disgrace him, he should listen to them, for they intend his good, as we learn in the chapter "Chelek" (Sanhedrin 105b): Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said, what is the meaning of what is written (Proverbs 27:6), "faithful are the wounds of a friend" etc.? Better the curse that Achiyah the Shilonite cursed Israel with than the blessing with which Balaam blessed them — Achiyah cursed them with a reed, as it is said (1 Kings 14:15), "and the LORD shall strike Israel as a reed sways in the water" — just as a reed stands in a place of water, its trunk sprouts anew and its roots are many, and even if all the winds come and blow upon it, it moves back and forth with them, but once they are calm it stands again in its place — so it is with Israel [resilient]. But the wicked Balaam blessed them with a cedar — just as a cedar does not stand in a place of water and its trunk does not sprout anew, and once a south wind blows upon it, it uproots it and overturns it — and this was the intent of the wicked Balaam even in his blessings, to uproot the enemies of Israel [i.e., Israel themselves]. And at a time when love and brotherhood dwell among Israel, the Holy One, blessed be He, comforts Zion and builds Jerusalem, and then there will be peace and tranquility in your palaces, as it is said (Psalms 122:8), "pray for the peace of Jerusalem, may those who love you be tranquil, peace be within your walls" etc., and it is written, "for the sake of my brothers and companions, let me now say, peace be within you." Thus far his words. Some of the statements he brought I omitted in copying, since they are well known and I did not wish to be so lengthy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:65: Here ends the discussion of the mitzvah of loving companions along the lines our Sages of blessed memory explained in the Midrashim. I further saw fit to speak of the matter of loving companions according to the way of the secret, as understood from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Zohar, and we shall explain this matter in a separate chapter, along with other matters that are great causes for nullifying anger, in order to give space between chapters:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:1: The reason for loving companions according to the way of the secret is this: since it is true and agreed by all that all souls are emanated from a high place, one must love the souls of all his companions insofar as they are a portion of God above, in the same reality by which he loves his own soul. And just as the supernal Godhead unites in the ultimate unity, so too the souls above have no envy, rivalry, or hatred, God forbid, for these attributes are external attributes of the external kelipah, but in holiness everything is in love, as we have elaborated in the Gate of Love, chapter 1 and chapter 6; see there. And although our Sages of blessed memory said (Bava Batra 75a; Zohar, portion Bereshit, 39a) that in the lower Garden of Eden each one is scorched by his companion's canopy, this is not out of hatred but rather he is embarrassed, thinking that he too should have attained that level where the supernal light would shine upon him more than it does — for this is the whole desire of the righteous in the Garden of Eden — thus we find that this is an envy that brings one to love of the Name, and he loves his fellow who merited that level through his deeds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:2: Now, for two reasons one must love his fellow — first, from the side of the soul, and second, from the side of the body — and regarding these two aspects it is possible that the prophet said (Malachi 2:10), "have we not all one father? Has not one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously, each against his brother?" And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained, "have we not all one father?" — this is Jacob our father, peace be upon him. And certainly this aspect is from the side of the body, for Jacob our father's bed was complete without any mixture of kelipah, and he merited to beget twelve tribes who produced seventy souls, all in holiness, none of them straying outside — and therefore Israel were then set apart from the other nations, since Jacob is "the cord of His inheritance," as explained in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 1; and therefore it is forbidden for us to intermarry with the other seventy nations. This is likewise explained in the Zohar (portion Acharei, 70b), which we copied in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 4, saying, fortunate are the righteous, etc., "their body is holy, their soul is holy."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:3: "Has not one God created us?" — "created us" is from the side of the soul, for the Creator, blessed be He, from the side of His spirituality, creates the souls, which are spiritual like Him, as explained (Niddah 31a), "three partners in man" etc., and the soul resembles the Holy One, blessed be He, in five things, as explained in the first chapter of Berachot (10a) regarding the five times "bless the LORD, O my soul" is said.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:4: And in the Ra'aya Meheimna (portion Pinchas, 246b) it is explained that "has not one God created us" alludes to two supernal [Names/aspects]. These are his words: another interpretation, "and he dreamed, and behold, a ladder" (Genesis 28:12) — the Faithful Shepherd, [the numerical value of] "sulam" [ladder] rises above all letters, so you do this — to rise above all creatures, in order to rise to the Name spelled Yod-Kei-Vav-Kei [each fully spelled out with alephs], within which is Yod-Yod-Yod [numerically], whose sum is [the equivalent of] "lamed" [30] — for at first you were in the Name Yod-Kei-Aleph Vav-Kei-Aleph, which is Yod-Aleph-Aleph-Aleph, within the thirteen measures of mercy which are "echad" [one]; now you shall rise to "El," which is Yod-Aleph-Yod [numerically forming Yah-El or similar] — for the two Names testify: "has not one God created us?" Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:5: When you examine what is explained in Tikkunim, that the two Names mentioned correspond to the body and the soul, and what is explained in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 7, our words here will become clear to you — that in the allusion of these words ["one father," "one God"] there is a shared participation in the creation of souls.
